title: Exports hit record  $ 15.28 b in 10 months; October tops $ 1.62 b | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 06:33
-     - 74

Sri Lanka’s export earnings reached a record $ 15.28 billion in the first months of 2026, up 6.03% year-on-year (YoY), supported by strong merchandise and services performance, while October also delivered the highest monthly export revenue on record at over $ 1.62 billion.

The latest data released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) yesterday showed October earnings grew by 11.57% YoY, with merchandise exports rising 9.65% YoY to over $ 1.26 billion, whilst the estimated service earnings in the month showed a growth of 18.87% YoY to $ 360.21 million.

However, total export earnings in October declined 8.69% month-on-month (MoM) decline compared with September 2026. 

Cumulative exports during the first 10 months saw merchandise export earnings increase by 5.72% YoY to over $ 12.01 billion, whilst services exports during the same period were estimated to have surged by 7.2% to $ 3.26 billion. Services exports include sectors such as ICT/BPM, construction, financial services, and transport and logistics.

“I am confident that Sri Lanka will achieve its $ 18 billion export earnings target for 2026 and could potentially exceed it,” EDB Chairman and CEO Mangala Wijesinghe told the Daily FT. 

He assured that the encouraging performance in October reflects the dedication of exporters and the growing potential of Sri Lankan products and services in international markets, the country could even do beyond $ 18 billion. 

However, he acknowledged that the country was unlikely to achieve the targeted 8-10% growth, with annual growth expected to be around 6.5%, citing the impact of the Middle East tensions and its direct impact on overall costs.

Addressing the media, Wijesinghe said moving forward, the priority must be to strengthen export competitiveness, diversify products and markets, enhance value addition, and accelerate innovation and technology adoption to create greater opportunities for Sri Lankan businesses.

The EDB noted that the merchandise exports growth in October was driven largely by improved demand across the agricultural and industrial product categories, along with service sectors. 

Cumulative export earnings from key value-added sectors was supported by strong performances in Electrical and Electronic Components (EEC) with 59.60% YoY to $ 566.14 million, spices and concentrates rose by 35.35% to $ 498.43 million, rubber-based exports increased by 101.10% YoY to $ 873.85 million and processed food and beverages rose by 18.93% to $ 594.52 million during January–October 2026.

However, the apparel and textiles sector declined by 5.50% YoY to over $ 4.19 billion during January–October 2026, compared with the corresponding period in 2025. This decline was driven by a 5.16% reduction in apparel exports to $ 3.89 billion and a 9.70% decrease in textile exports to $ 299.26 million. 

Wijesinghe said the sector’s performance was affected by subdued demand in key export markets, particularly the US and the European Union (EU), which together account for more than half of Sri Lanka’s apparel exports.

Tea export earnings declined by 6.77% YoY to $ 1.2 billion during January–October 2026. The decline was mainly driven by lower earnings from tea packets and bulk tea, which decreased by 5.18% and 10.37%, respectively.

The US, Sri Lanka’s largest single export destination, accounting for around 21% of total merchandise exports, recorded YoY growth of 7.77% in October 2026, with export earnings reaching $ 265.32 million. Cumulative exports to the US during January–October 2026 also increased marginally by 0.81% YoY, reaching $ 2.51 billion. This performance reinforces the continued importance of the US market to Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports, maintaining its position as the country’s leading export destination.

India overtook the UK to become Sri Lanka’s second-largest export destination, with cumulative exports increasing 14.16% to $ 989.66 million during the first 10 months of 2026. October exports to India surged 34% YoY to $ 99.82 million. 

In contrast, exports to the UK fell 1.88% YoY to $ 69.04 million in October, while cumulative earnings declined 8.67% to $ 723.40 million.

Exports to the European Union (EU), which accounted for 21.57% of Sri Lanka’s total merchandise exports during January–October 2026, registered a YoY decline of 6.64% in October 2026, with export earnings amounting to $ 265.14 million. Cumulative exports to the EU during January–October 2026 also declined marginally by 0.85% YoY, reaching $ 2.59 billion.

title: Sri Lanka spared as US targets major trading partners with new tariffs | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 06:47
-     - 38

Sri Lanka has been left out of the latest round of US tariff measures targeting several major trading partners, including China, India, the European Union (EU), Vietnam and Bangladesh.

The new tariffs, announced by the White House following investigations into the trade practices of 14 economies, are set to affect some of the US’ biggest trading partners, with rates ranging from 20% to as high as 40%.

China faces the steepest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, while other affected economies face rates of 20% or 25%. However, the effective rates for some countries will be lower due to tariff caps agreed by US President Donald Trump.

The 14 economies covered by the investigations are China, India, the EU, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India. Sri Lanka is not among those named.

The latest move follows the US Supreme Court ruling that Trump’s previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal, prompting the administration to pursue alternative trade measures.

The investigations were launched in March under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, which examines whether foreign government policies and practices unfairly disadvantage American businesses, workers and consumers.

Trump has repeatedly used tariffs as a central plank of his trade policy, arguing they would encourage domestic manufacturing and create jobs. However, economists have warned that import duties could raise consumer prices, fuel inflation and weigh on global trade.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has pressed for faster allocation of land to investors, saying tax concessions alone are not enough to attract investment while the process of obtaining land takes about 18 months, the Parliament Secretariat said.

The President made the remarks at a meeting of the Ministerial Consultative Committee on Finance, Planning and Economic Development, held under his chairmanship at Parliament on Monday.

The Committee discussed identifying State-owned land and placing it under the purview of the Board of Investment (BOI) or a specialised land bank. Such land would then be allocated faster through a mechanism based on the scale of investment, the employment generated and the potential impact on the national economy.

The President also called for faster district-level development projects and more efficient management of public funds. He said ministries and institutions should prepare plans to implement their projects from the start of each financial year and review progress monthly.

President presses...

Funds unutilised at the end of the year can be carried forward only if specific conditions are met, such as the opening of letters of credit (LCs) for the relevant projects, he said. Otherwise, the allocations must be returned to the General Treasury and fresh allocations made in the following year’s Budget. He stressed the need to monitor progress at district level, based on the project report books provided to District Development Committees.

The Committee also discussed fertiliser subsidies for farmers and the management of the Maha season paddy harvest. It highlighted the need to clear paddy stocks remaining in storage before the next Maha harvest arrives, and considered converting existing stocks into rice for distribution through welfare programs, or using them for animal feed and other products.

Cryptocurrency regulation, the digitalisation of the insurance and transactions sectors, and VAT-related issues faced by cooperative societies were also discussed.

The meeting was attended by Labour Minister and Deputy Finance and Planning Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha, Economic Development Deputy Minister Nishantha Jayaweera, Members of Parliament, and officials of the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development.

title: Unchecked cheap foreign tea imports threaten ‘total collapse’ of SL plantation economy: PA | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 06:41
-     - 23

The Planters’ Association of Ceylon (PA) yesterday raised alarm bells over what it calls the unhindered and rampant importation of cheap foreign teas into the country.

“The Association warns that allowing low-cost, external teas to be brought in, blended and re-exported under the Sri Lankan flag is systematically undermining the hard-earned equity of Pure Ceylon Tea, devastating local livelihoods and driving the domestic plantation economy toward total decline,” the PA said in a statement.

It said that for generations, Ceylon Tea’s global reputation has commanded a premium in international markets, strictly on the strength of its unique, single-origin provenance, rigorous quality standards and geographical indication. The PA cautioned that flooding the domestic supply chain with cheap foreign alternatives dilutes this core unique selling proposition (USP), risking irreversible damage to consumer trust worldwide.

Today, Sri Lanka’s tea industry sits at a sharp, structural crossroads: it commands premium global prices for its orthodox teas, yet its cost of production is roughly 2.5 to 3.1 times higher than that of major rivals India and Kenya, while over 70% of its output depends on fragmented smallholder plots facing severe input and labour pressures.

Furthermore, the influx of external teas creates artificial downward pressure at the Colombo Tea Auction, the world’s largest single-origin tea trading platform. Depressed Net Sale Averages (NSAs) directly compress green leaf payout rates, delivering an immediate and severe financial blow to over 400,000 smallholder farming families and regional plantation workers who are already struggling with escalating living and operational costs.

Under the governing statutory framework, specifically the Sri Lanka Tea Board (SLTB) Import and Export Regulations, the gazette regulations mandated a fixed, rigid 70:30 ratio for mixing imported tea with locally grown tea.

The framework states that import permits for blending and re-export are contingent upon the condition that “the imported tea is blended with tea produced within Sri Lanka, and such tea has been purchased at the Colombo tea auctions or from any other industry approved channel of sale.”

This is to safeguard the Ceylon Tea identity, for which the SLTB must use its authority to ensure that imported teas function strictly as minority components. They must be mixed with a sufficiently high proportion of local tea so that the final exported package qualifies to carry an approved mandatory label such as “A blend of Ceylon tea and tea of other origin packed in Sri Lanka”, ensuring the bulk of the product remains rooted in local production.

Other than specialty teas, the cheap, poor-quality teas imported at around $ 1.20 per kg for value addition are detrimental to the image of Ceylon Tea.

The core grievance of local producers is straightforward: importing foreign tea does not complement the domestic industry; it cannibalises it.

For over a century, the words “Ceylon Tea” have conjured images of misty mountain slopes, hand-plucked golden tips and uncompromising purity. Yet beneath the global prestige of the island’s premier export lies a quiet, bruising economic war.

By contrast, Kenya and India produce tea at a fraction of that cost, $ 1 to $ 1.25 per kg, due to high-yield clonal varieties on flat terrain and mechanised harvesting. Allowing blenders to access these cheap foreign inputs removes the commercial pressure to buy local green leaf, leaving growers to absorb losses as well as the burden of unsold produce, which they cannot afford.

Under normal market conditions, unsold lots at the Colombo Tea Auction typically account for approximately 5% to 8% of total weekly offerings, which generally range between 5 and 6 MnKg.

However, following the influx of cheaper, inferior-quality imported teas at around $ 1.20 per kg, the out-lot percentage increased significantly to approximately 25%, with the impact particularly pronounced in the case of CTC teas.

In late 2025, following the abolition of the Simplified Value Added Tax (SVAT) scheme in October 2025, exporters cut back on holding inventory due to upfront VAT cash-flow costs, driving unsold volumes significantly higher alongside an immediate Rs. 100 per kg drop in auction prices.

In March 2026, following the escalation of the US-Israel-Iran conflict and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz (affecting 70% of Sri Lanka’s export destinations), unsold lots jumped to 15% to 18% of weekly offerings, or 0.8 to 1 MnKg per week. Throughout mid-to-late 2026 (June to November), weekly broker reports repeatedly flagged that a ‘greater majority’ of Nuwara Eliya, Uda Pussellawa and Western BOP/BOPF teas remained unsold due to a lack of suitable bids.

Will this ultimately kill the plantation industry?

The PA warned that if current trends persist without structural reform, the importation and blending model risks triggering a slow-motion collapse of the domestic upstream sector:

The abandonment crisis: Faced with meagre green leaf returns that fail to cover the cost of fertiliser and labour, a growing number of smallholders are uprooting tea bushes to switch to more lucrative crops such as cinnamon or rubber, or abandoning their lands entirely.

A hollowed-out exporter economy: If local green leaf production continues to stagnate or decline due to a lack of upstream investment, Sri Lanka risks transforming from an agricultural producer into a mere transit-and-repackaging terminal. While packing factories might survive on imported Indian and Kenyan raw material, the actual plantation economy, the hills, the estates and the rural communities, will wither away.

Conclusion

The PA said the debate over tea imports forces Sri Lanka to confront a stark identity crisis: will it remain a proud agricultural nation anchored in the heritage of Pure Ceylon Tea, or will it become a commoditised blending hub competing on cheap volume against giants it cannot out-produce?

For the hundreds of thousands of growers whose survival depends on every single kilogram of green leaf, the answer is clear. Unless policymakers fiercely protect farm-gate prices, restrict import loopholes and aggressively reinvest in domestic replanting and productivity, the legacy of Ceylon Tea may well be harvested to its grave, the PA said.

title: Tea exports fall 7% in Oct.; dollar prices edge up | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 06:39
-     - 19

Tea exports fell 7% year-on-year to 20.4 MnKg in October from 21.9 MnKg, but export prices edged up in dollar terms, according to Sri Lanka Customs data analysed by Forbes & Walker Research and Asia Siyaka Commodities PLC’s Siyaka Research.

“The continued impact of the Iran crisis, coupled with lower tea production arising from adverse weather conditions, has weighed on export volumes, bringing October shipments to their lowest level in three months,” Siyaka Research said.

Forbes & Walker Research data show the average Free on Board (FOB) value, the export price before freight and insurance, rose to $ 5.81 per kg in October from $ 5.78 a year earlier, and to Rs. 1,924.15 per kg from Rs. 1,752.65. Packeted tea rose to $ 5.55 per kg from $ 5.45 and tea bags to $ 9.31 from $ 8.81, while bulk tea eased to $ 4.61 from $ 4.74.

Volumes in October diverged by category. “Tea in Bulk, Instant Tea and Green Tea have recorded positive variances against the corresponding period of the previous year, whilst Tea Packets and Tea Bags recorded negative variances,” Forbes & Walker Research said. Packeted tea fell to 8.4 MnKg from 10.4 MnKg and tea bags to 2.3 MnKg from 2.6 MnKg, while bulk tea rose to 8.6 MnKg from 8.3 MnKg.

For the first 10 months of 2026, exports reached 209.8 MnKg, 5% below the 220.2 MnKg shipped in the same period of 2025. Siyaka Research said rupee earnings were marginally higher at Rs. 389.5 billion, against Rs. 389.3 billion a year earlier, largely because the rupee depreciated against the dollar. In dollar terms, earnings fell to $ 1.2 billion from $ 1.28 billion.

The cumulative average FOB value fell to $ 5.73 per kg from $ 5.86, even as it rose to Rs. 1,856.12 from Rs. 1,754.28 in rupee terms. Forbes & Walker Research said only tea bags gained in dollar terms over the 10 months, rising to $ 9.39 per kg from $ 9.26.

Value-added tea accounted for 58% of shipments over the period, marginally below 59% a year earlier, mainly because fewer packeted teas were exported, Siyaka Research said. Tea bags held at about 10% of exports, although volumes fell 4% to 21.4 MnKg. Instant tea rose 30% to 3.5 MnKg and green tea held steady at 4.3 MnKg.

The market rankings shifted sharply. Türkiye was the largest buyer over the 10 months, with shipments rising 119% to 38.8 MnKg from 17.7 MnKg. Iraq, the top market in the same period last year according to Siyaka Research, fell 41% to 20.1 MnKg from 33.9 MnKg. Russia was third with 19 MnKg, up 3.3%, followed by Azerbaijan, up 26% to 9.5 MnKg, and China, down 9% to 7.9 MnKg.

Forbes & Walker Research said Syria overtook Libya for sixth place with 7.5 MnKg, up 4.7%, while Libya’s purchases plunged 58% to 7.3 MnKg. Chile moved up to eighth with 7.2 MnKg despite a 25% fall, Saudi Arabia held ninth with 6.8 MnKg, down 6%, and Jordan dropped to 10th with 6.8 MnKg.

“The overall export performance during the first ten months reflects the combined pressures of weaker production, geopolitical uncertainties and softer earnings in US Dollar terms,” Siyaka Research said.

title: Ambeon ties private placement to fully subscribed Rs. 4 b Rights | Daily FT

Thursday, 26 November 2026 06:38

Ambeon Capital PLC will go ahead with its proposed private placement of shares only if its Rights Issue is fully subscribed, and will offer the placement shares only to those who take up the Rights, the company said yesterday.

The company first announced the capital raising on 17 July, 2026, with plans to raise up to Rs. 4 billion. The rights issue covers up to 100 million ordinary voting shares at Rs. 32 each, raising up to Rs. 3.2 billion, with existing shareholders entitled to one new share for every 10.22352863 shares held. The private placement covers up to 25 million ordinary voting shares at the same price of Rs. 32, raising a further Rs. 800 million.

The change, decided by the Board on 2 September, 2026, alters the structure and sequence of the capital raising first announced on 17 July, 2026.

Subscribers include both existing shareholders and investors who buy rights on the Colombo Stock Exchange during the rights trading period, and they must apply specifically for the placement shares.

“The issue of the Private Placement Shares will be at the option of the Board of Directors and contingent on the full subscription of the Rights Issue and the receipt of applications for the Private Placement Shares,” the company said. It added that it would not proceed with the placement if the rights issue is undersubscribed or if no applications are received.

The Colombo Stock Exchange granted in-principle approval for the rights issue and private placement on 21 October, 2026. An extraordinary general meeting (EGM) on 22 December, 2026 will seek shareholder approval for the rights issue only. The shares will trade ex-rights from 24 December, with the record date and provisional allotment on 28 December and rights deposited into shareholders’ Central Depository System (CDS) accounts on 31 December.

Provisional letters of allotment will be dispatched on 5 January, 2027, together with application forms for the placement shares, which will also be available on the company’s website. Trading in rights begins on 11 January, the last date for renunciation is 19 January, and the deadline for acceptance and payment for rights, and for placement applications, is 25 January.

If the Board decides to proceed, it will announce the decision together with the level of subscription to the rights issue, and will then tell each applicant how many placement shares they have been allocated and what they must pay. Once the new rights shares are listed, a separate EGM will be called to approve the placement by special resolution. Payment will be due by the fifth market day after that meeting.

The company set strict terms for late or missing payments. “In the event any applicants do not pay the consideration for the Private Placement Shares allocated to them by the payment cut off time, such Private Placement Shares allocated will not be issued to such applicants and will not be reallocated to any other person,” it said. Monies paid after the cut-off will be refunded within three market days, and the placement will then be undersubscribed.

Ambeon also ruled out using the funds to cut its borrowings. “The proceeds of the Private Placement will be utilised solely for the purpose of making new equity investments in high growth future focused ventures in sectors such as financial services, technology, real estate and fast moving consumer goods (FMCG). No proceeds will be used to reduce the gearing ratio of the Company by settlement of any debt of the Company,” the company said.

The group reported assets of Rs. 6.61 per share as of end-September 2026 with top shareholder at the time being Ambeon Consolidated (50.16%) followed by ARRC Capital (13.28%) and ATX Partners (9.80%) with a public float of 18.01%.

title: UN-Government initiative strengthens social dialogue to build trust and prevent conflict | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 06:13
-     - 13

By Amira Cader

From left: UN Resident Coordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche, Public Administration, Provincial Councils and Local Government Ministry Secretary S. Alokabandara, UNESCO Regional Office for South Asia Chief of Sector and Program Specialist Eunsong Kim (Moderator), Uva Workers Development Foundation Founder Vadival Anthony, and MAS Holdings Gender Equality Head Thanuja Jayawardene

– Pic by Lasantha Kumara

Sri Lanka’s economic crisis brought more than financial hardship. It also placed pressure on workplaces, public institutions and relationships within communities, highlighting the need for stronger dialogue to address grievances, prevent disputes and rebuild trust.

Against this backdrop, a two-year initiative by the United Nations and the Government of Sri Lanka has sought to make social dialogue a practical tool for strengthening institutions, improving workplace relations and promoting social cohesion.

The Social Dialogue for Peace and Crisis Prevention in Sri Lanka project, implemented by the International Labour Organisation (ILO), the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), with funding from the UN Sri Lanka SDG Fund, concluded its activities at Cinnamon Grand Colombo yesterday.

The initiative brought together Government, employers, trade unions, civil society organisations and communities, creating opportunities for people to raise concerns and have a say in decisions affecting their lives.

UN Resident Coordinator in Sri Lanka Marc-André Franche said the project had helped move relationships between workers, the State and communities away from confrontation towards constructive dialogue.

He recalled that the initiative was conceived during the economic crisis, when public institutions were under considerable pressure. Between 2021 and 2023, around 2,700 labour-related registrations were recorded in sectors including postal services, railways, health and energy, highlighting the need for effective mechanisms to address workplace concerns before they escalated.

One of the project’s major achievements was the establishment of a structured national framework for dialogue covering approximately 1.4 million public-sector employees. Described as the first framework of its kind in South Asia, it operates through 82 workplace forums, seven sectoral forums and a National Public Sector Dialogue Forum.

Franche said more than half of the disputes raised through workplace forums had been resolved locally without escalation. He also highlighted a reduction in public-sector protests from 51 in 2022 to eight in 2025, alongside the wider economic recovery.

A wage dispute at Sri Lanka Railways, resolved through dialogue before developing into a strike, was cited as an example of how early engagement could prevent disruptions to essential services.

He stressed that industrial disputes affect not only workers and employers but also public services and economic activity, potentially affecting investor confidence. As Sri Lanka continues its recovery and public-sector reforms, trusted channels for discussing issues such as wages, working conditions and administrative changes will become increasingly important.

Gender equality and workplace safety were also important areas of the initiative. More than 1,400 public officials across 72 workplace forums in six ministries received training on addressing gender equality, safety and dignity at work.

The Postal Department is developing a gender-responsive action plan, while the Ministry of Transport has introduced mandatory gender and safety training for public transport workers.

In the private sector, 25 companies and 350 employers engaged with trade union representatives through the project, with support from the Employers’ Federation of Ceylon, the UN Global Compact Network Sri Lanka and the National Labour Advisory Council.

The initiative also focused on strengthening grievance mechanisms, preventing workplace sexual harassment and encouraging women’s participation in leadership.

Discussions at the closing event highlighted why gender equality requires more than policies against discrimination and harassment. Organisations need to examine recruitment, promotions, training and leadership opportunities to understand the barriers that continue to limit women’s progress.

Addressing unconscious bias, providing regular training and creating safe channels for employees to raise concerns were identified as important steps. Workplace policies, participants stressed, must be supported by action, open communication and management commitment.

The project also extended its work to communities, particularly groups that are often left out of decision-making.

With UNESCO working alongside the Centre for Poverty Analysis, the Coalition for Inclusive Impact and World Vision Lanka, 33 community forums were supported across Gampaha, Badulla and Batticaloa.

More than 180 forum members received training to better understand policymaking processes and communicate community priorities to district-level officials.

The forums enabled people from fisheries, plantation and agricultural communities to raise concerns directly with public authorities. In Batticaloa and Jaffna, discussions also brought attention to longstanding issues, including land rights and language access affecting Tamil-speaking communities.

Policy briefs on these concerns were presented to parliamentary sectoral committees, with further engagement involving relevant ministries continuing.

A key highlight of the closing event was a panel discussion titled ‘Dialogue in Action: Reflecting on the Impact of Social Dialogue’, moderated by UNESCO Regional Office for South Asia Chief of Sector and Program Specialist Eusong Kim.

The panel featured UN Resident Coordinator Marc-André Franche, Public Administration Ministry Secretary S. Aloka Bandara, Vadivel Anthony and MAS Holdings Women Go Beyond Head Thanuja Jayawardena, bringing together Government, UN and private-sector perspectives.

The discussion focused on how social dialogue could support public-sector reforms, improve workplace cooperation and strengthen social cohesion.

Particular attention was given to ensuring that public servants have opportunities to express their concerns and participate in decisions affecting their working conditions, especially as administrative reforms continue.

The private-sector perspective highlighted the need to address workplace attitudes and unconscious bias that can limit women’s opportunities, while strengthening systems through which employees can report concerns and seek fair solutions.

Franche said differences of opinion should not automatically be treated as a problem. In a diverse society, disagreements are inevitable, but institutions must provide spaces where people can express different views, challenge prejudice and work towards solutions.

He also pointed to the need for wider public consultation in policymaking, including the national budget process, stressing that meaningful participation should go beyond formal parliamentary discussions.

He explained that the United Nations’ role was not to dictate what Sri Lanka should do, but to facilitate discussions, create opportunities for engagement and bring international expertise in mediation and negotiation.

Looking ahead, Franche identified the forthcoming expiry of plantation company estate leases, covering approximately one-fifth of Sri Lanka’s arable land, as an opportunity to address longstanding inequalities and improve employment opportunities for plantation workers.

He also stressed the importance of ensuring that women and young people remain involved in decision-making and that community platforms and institutional mechanisms continue beyond the project’s lifespan.

Another important message from the closing remarks was that the initiative’s contribution went beyond the forums, training programs and activities established over two years. The trust, relationships and shared understanding developed between Government, employers, workers and communities were equally important.

The speakers expressed appreciation to the Public Administration Ministry for its leadership and coordination, as well as to the trade union partners, development organisations, participating institutions and communities.

Although the project has formally concluded, its work is far from over. Its success will ultimately depend on whether the dialogue mechanisms become part of everyday institutional practice and continue to give people a meaningful voice.

For Sri Lanka, the challenge now is to keep those conversations going. Lasting peace is not built simply by avoiding disagreements but by creating the trust and understanding needed to address them together.

As Niccolo Machiavelli observed, only those at the base can see what the apex is like. Only the ruled know what the rulers are like. Centuries later, Marxism elaborated the point philosophically and epistemologically. Capitalism can be understood as a totality only by those who view it, not necessarily from the lived personal experience, but from the standpoint and perspective of the working classes—the majority within the system, at the base

Whenever President AKD and his Cabinet colleagues scoff in Parliament and at public meetings at the notion of a debt burden/repayment problem, saying it is all under control, they simply aren’t telling the truth.

One of our most eminent economists, ANU’s Prof Emeritus Prema-chandra Athukorala blew the whistle, calling the repayment agreement “a sword of Damocles”.

‘…He attributed this to a restructuring that relied on maturity extensions and coupon (interest rate) cuts rather than haircuts, or write-downs, on International Sovereign Bonds (ISBs). Ghana, by contrast, secured a haircut of about 37% from its bondholders in 2024. Sri Lanka’s upfront debt service relief of about $ 3 billion could fall to $ 1.8 billion under the new macro-linked bonds if growth exceeds the IMF baseline, or rise to $ 4.3 billion if it falls short.

“Paradoxically, therefore, stronger-than-anticipated economic growth could itself increase the debt-servicing burden,” he said.

Annual debt service payments (principal and interest) have climbed from $ 2.8 billion in 2023 to $ 4.3 billion in 2024 and $ 5.1 billion in 2025, with the Government accounting for 47% of the 2025 total.

The debt service ratio, debt service as a share of exports, rose from 15.9% to 24.9% over the same period.

Prof. Athukorala said the ratio had already reached the pre-crisis level as repayment of past due interest (PDI) bonds began in 2025. It would rise further once ISB coupon payments resume after 2027.

“The central concern is that borrowing at such high interest rates would perpetuate the debt overhang, leaving a sword of Damocles hanging over the country’s economic future and risking a trajectory of recurrent debt crises similar to Argentina’s,” he said.

(https://www.ft.lk/top-story/Sri-Lanka-will-exit-IMF-program-with-debt-overhang-intact-Economist/26-800424)

President AKD’s unprecedented, needless induction of the Chairman of the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, which also contained ISB holders, as one of his two Economic advisors and a negotiator with the IMF and private foreign ISB holders, wasn’t smart.

WAW and Walt Rostow

I was amazed and amused to read Dr WA Wijewardena recommending Walt Rostow’s ‘The Stages of Economic Growth: An Anti-Communist Manifesto’, to President Anura Dissanayake, adding that when he was a student of economics in the 1960s, Rostow was a ‘hero’. (https://www.dailymirror.lk/business/Wijewardena-urges-AKD-to-follow-Rostows-Non-Communist-Manifesto-for-take-off/215-355071)

Among the best and brightest of Ceylonese economists of the 1960s, he wasn’t.

Though only a (precocious) boy, I got around quite a bit with my father and was in the room or restaurant when he was in conversation with his personal friends who were top economic thinkers and policy-makers: Gamani Corea, Godfrey Gunatilleke, Lal Jayawardena, Jayantha Kelegama, Nihal Kappagoda, David Loos to name a few. Their main concerns were Development (as distinct from mere ‘Growth’), greater autonomy for the Third World, and social welfare to maintain a decent, rising Quality of Life for the people. JK Galbraith and Raul Prebisch were among the giants in vogue at the time. Back issues of the MARGA journal would trace the intellectual lineage of the economic thinking of the day.

As for university students in the 1960s, they rebelled violently twice, clashing with the Police and the Army at Colombo and Peradeniya. I doubt my old friend, Economics student at Peradeniya in the mid-1960s, N. Shanmugaratnam, currently Professor Emeritus of Development Studies at a Norwegian university, ever regarded Rostow ‘a hero’.

The Ceylonese intelligentsia and university student community of the 1960s opposed America’s Cold War policy as emblematised by the Vietnam War. Rostow’s ‘Stages of Economic Growth’ was recognised as a counter-revolutionary, indeed counter-reform, manifesto for US policy in the Third World during the Cold War.

The 1960s paradigm was, quite rightly, not ‘Growth’ per se, but ‘Development’. The centre of intellectual inspiration for the English-speaking policy intelligentsia—French and Spanish speaking policy intellectuals were way ahead of the Commonwealth ones—was the Institute of Development Studies (IDS), Sussex. It was Dudley Seers, Michael Lipton and Richard Jolly who were most respected by Ceylonese economists.

When Asia had its economic miracle, LSE’s Prof Robert Wade was its most outstanding theoretical interpreter with ‘Governing the Market: Economic Theory and the Role of Government in East Asia’s Industrialisation’ (Princeton 1990). The East Asian miracle bore no resemblance to Walt Rostow’s  ‘Stages of Economic Growth’.

Nobel Prize winners Joe Stiglitz and Paul Krugman never mention Rostow’s book approvingly.

Counter-diagnosis

Budget 2027 gave rise to two expected sets of responses: on the one hand that of the Establishment, i.e., the President and Government, top corporates, neoliberal economists, and international investment ‘experts’, and on the other hand, the Parliamentary Opposition.

The economic policy elite which for the first time since 1948 overlaps with the actual economic elite, commended the President and Govt for the Budget, but urged expeditious movement along the same trajectory, to free or minimise exchange controls and liberalise labour and land laws. (https://www.ft.lk/top-story/Sri-Lanka-must-prove-recovery-is-more-than-a-cycle-Hosking/26-800322)

In 2017, under the Yahapalanaya UNP, the foreign exchange controls of 1950s were relaxed with no benefit to the country. Further relaxation to the point of near-absence of foreign exchange controls would facilitate rather than inhibit capital flight.

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa directed a withering critique at the President’s Budget and its social impacts.

However, the Opposition as a whole didn’t address and rule out some of the more drastic neoliberal measures lobbied for by the economic elite—such as a return to the international money markets, further liberalisation of exchange controls, and ‘liberalisation’ of labour and land laws. The parameters of the alternative economic policy of the Opposition are as yet unknown.

A Third Perspective from outside the economic and political establishments including the parliamentary Opposition, coming from ‘the Movement’, contains an intellectually serious, impressive analysis. The clearest scan of and sharpest scalpel dissecting the Budget was a substantive statement signed by a network of 38 trade unions and civic organisations, calling itself ‘Trade Unions and People’s Power!’. (2027 Budget: Red herring to neutralise public and relink Sri Lanka with new financial colonialism | Daily FT)

The necessary convergence of academically-trained intellect and organised wage-earners has  commenced. I gather that Dhanusha Pathirana, co-author of the book ‘A History of Underdevelopment and Political Economy of Inflation in Sri Lanka’ (Palgrave Macmillan, UK), is a member of the network and a principal author of this high-quality text.

The analysis contains a penetrating diagnosis and makes a logical, credible, extremely disturbing case.

Here are the key take-aways from the text, in its own words, reproduced as bullet points. All bullet-points in this column are direct excerpts.

The Government is deliberately underspending Budget allocations to create surpluses that would help Sri Lanka return to International Sovereign Bond (ISB) markets under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) program.

While Sri Lanka’s corporate sector benefits by maintaining enormous tax breaks… crumbs [are] thrown to the general public through indirect tax relief on a few essentials. Reducing taxes on sprats, dry fish and exercise books—alongside nominal salary increases for Government servants—will do nothing to halt the worsening living costs or reverse the steep cuts in essential spending mandated by the 2027 proposals.

Hyper-inflationary indirect taxes are set to escalate by Rs. 170 billion, while the increase in direct tax income will be negligible at Rs. 30 billion, worsening the ratio between the two components to around 80% from 78% this year.

Subsidies and transfers are slashed brutally by a staggering Rs. 100 billion (dropping from Rs. 1.57 trillion to Rs. 1.47 trillion)—showing total disregard for mass poverty at 16% according to the Ministry of Health and malnutrition among school children as high as 25% (UNICEF Sri Lanka).

Corporate income tax holidays, on the other hand, which cost a mammoth Rs. 190 billion in 2024/25 according to the Ministry of Finance Tax Expenditure Report, continue unabated.

85% of the burden of the expected tax revenue increase falls squarely on the general public.

The statement sets out the cumulative negative consequences of Budget 2027 policies.

Higher indirect taxes and soaring living costs also restricts productive investments. Higher living costs inevitably fuel wage demands, inflating production costs without raising real wages. This erodes the competitive power of domestic producers in both domestic and global markets, accelerating the flight of manufacturing investments, while driving speculative and foreign-exchange-draining capital into property and real estate and illicit capital flows to hedge against inflation.

‘Trade Unions and People’s Power’ recommend alternative policies which would bring greater benefits.

Shifting towards a higher direct-to-indirect tax ratio by revoking corporate income tax breaks and enforcing strict tax compliance would ease the cost of living, curb inflation, and lift families out of poverty and child malnutrition, while improving fiscal stability.

It would drive down interest rates and hence, Government debt-servicing costs, while stimulating real investments, creating a virtuous cycle that further expands direct tax revenue through rising aggregate incomes.

Yet, the current tax policy remains entirely geared towards speculative and commercial capital that prefers shifting assets and surpluses abroad or into real estate rather than expanding industry.

That the Government has eschewed these options reveals the socioeconomic interests that the AKD-JVP-NPP administration primarily serves.

Going beyond the parliamentary Opposition, the TU Statement argues that the current tax policy actually ‘locks in economic backwardness’ and ‘structural stagnation’.

Consequently, the tax structure locks in economic backwardness. This is underscored by Sri Lanka’s Economic Complexity Index rank remaining stagnant at 83rd globally, with its value trapped in negative territory (-0.045) since the inception of the index in the mid-1990s.

The 2027 Budget will ensure that this structural stagnation in the economy persists.

The ‘Movement’ statement then proceeds, as the parliamentary Opposition does not, to unmask what the Government is actually doing: the deliberate ‘manufacture’ of ‘artificial’ budget surpluses.

Essential public investments (excluding highways and expressways) are choked through relentless and deliberate underspending. This has become the trademark strategy of the current administration: neutralise public outrage through exaggerated spending figures during Budget speeches, and…brutally underspending budgetary allocations to manufacture artificial budget surpluses.

The current Government utilised only 8% of the funds allocated for Cyclone Ditwah victims by mid-2026, according to the World Bank. By overachieving revenue targets and underspending 2026 budgetary allocations by roughly Rs. 1 trillion compared to the proposed Rs. 7 trillion, the Government has manufactured a surplus of Rs. 22 billion on the back of neglected public services.

Slashing Government spending and raising regressive taxes are manoeuvres designed solely to lower the risk premiums demanded by international finance capital.

Given Prof Prema-chandra Athukorala’s dire warning about ‘debt overhang’, this is suicidal.

The statement’s diagnostics yield this conclusion:

…the regime’s alliance with a broadly unproductive, hyper-consumerist business elite prevents it from imposing exchange controls, halting illicit capital outflows to boost national savings destroyed through hyper-consumerism and resolving the balance of payments (BoP) crisis without resorting to speculative foreign financing through ISBs (rising BoP issues are indicated by the deficit in the current account recording over $ 400 million in the first nine months of 2026).

AKD-JVP-NPP’s true character

As Niccolo Machiavelli observed, only those at the base can see what the apex is like. Only the ruled know what the rulers are like.

title: Less goods, not just more money: Why tighter credit alone could make our inflation worse | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 03:50
-     - 23

CBSL Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe

The Central Bank has raised interest rates and locked away more of the banks’ deposits. The diagnosis behind these moves is that too much money is chasing too few goods. But our inflation is coming mainly from fuel, transport and food. Treat a supply problem as a money problem, and we risk shutting down the very businesses that produce what we buy

The Central Bank’s Financial Stability Review 2026 was an alarm. Credit is growing far faster than deposits, and much of it is flowing into consumption rather than production. A Central Bank must act early rather than clean up later. It has now acted.

On 20 November, the Central Bank raised its Overnight Policy Rate by 25 basis points to 9%, its second increase this year after a 100 basis point rise in May. It also raised the Statutory Reserve Ratio from 2% to 3%, effective from 9 December. The Governor expects inflation, already 8.5% in November, to reach about 9% by December.

I welcome a Central Bank that acts rather than waits. But in medicine, the treatment is only as good as the diagnosis. Give a patient the wrong medicine and the illness can get worse. That is my concern today.

What the Central Bank has done

The two measures work in different ways, but they aim at the same thing: less money in circulation and slower credit.

The Central Bank’s reasoning rests on two points. First, credit to the private sector is still growing fast. Second, its purchases of foreign currency to rebuild reserves have released a large amount of rupee liquidity into the money market, which could keep that credit growing. Both points are fair.

Too much money, or too few goods?

We all learned the textbook definition: inflation is too much money chasing too few goods. We tend to remember only the first half. But the definition has two halves, and either one can drive prices up. Prices rise when money grows faster than goods. They also rise when goods become scarce or more expensive to produce, even if money does not grow at all.

Look at where today’s inflation is actually coming from.

Transport prices are up 17.6% in a year. Restaurants and hotels are up 13.4%. Food is up 8.8%, driven by big onions, fresh fish, eggs, bread, wheat flour, chicken, milk powder and coconuts. Yet core inflation, which strips out food, energy and transport, is only 5.6%.

In other words, most of our inflation is not coming from money. It is coming from fuel, freight and food.

The Central Bank itself says as much. It points to the Middle East conflict and high global energy prices, the rising cost of food, and the second-round effects of earlier energy price increases. These are supply shocks. They begin outside our banking system, and no amount of tightening inside it will produce a liter of fuel or a kilo of onions.

The trend over the year tells the same story. Until March, headline and core inflation moved together, at around 2%. In April, as the energy shock hit, prices of non-food items jumped and headline inflation leapt ahead. It has stayed well above core inflation ever since. If too much money were the main cause, core inflation would be rising just as fast.

The credit boom is real, too

I do not dismiss the demand side. The Central Bank’s own Financial Stability Review sets out the numbers, and they are stark.

Bank credit grew 23.6% year-on-year in the second quarter, while retail deposits grew only 6.7%. The Credit-to-Deposit Ratio reached 74%. Pawning advances surged 49.2%. Consumption loans now make up 19.5% of bank lending, against about 11% for SMEs and 8.7% for agriculture.

So we have both problems at once: a supply shock pushing prices up, and a consumer credit boom adding fuel to the fire. The question is not whether the Central Bank should act. It is whether the tools it has chosen hit the right target.

Mixed signals

On the same day the Central Bank raised rates and reserves, the Governor told reporters that the Central Bank has no target for credit growth. Credit growing at more than 20% was, in his words, “a very good provision of credit to the economy”. He rejected suggestions that people should delay taking loans: at current rates, he said, “one should definitely take a loan”, provided it is backed by a genuine need and the capacity to repay. As a banker I understand the point. Credit backed by repayment capacity is the lifeblood of an economy. But the message to the market is mixed. The Central Bank is locking away deposits to slow lending, while telling the public that borrowing is a good idea. Banks will hear the first message through their costs. Borrowers will hear the second through the headlines.

More importantly, repayment capacity tells us whether a loan will be repaid. It does not tell us what the loan is for. A pawning loan against a gold chain is easy to repay, because the bank holds the gold. A vehicle loan backed by a fixed salary scores well. A manufacturer’s working capital loan, with cash flows that depend on orders and energy costs, often scores worse. If repayment capacity is the only test, credit will keep flowing to consumption and away from production. That is exactly what the Financial Stability Review shows.

A Central Bank with no view on the direction of credit is leaving that choice to the collateral.

The Governor says the Central Bank watches how borrowing affects aggregate demand, particularly for imports. That is the right lens. But a loan that finances an imported car and a loan that finances a local onion farmer have very different effects on imports and on prices. The lens is right. It needs to look at where the credit goes, not only how much of it there is.

How the banks will absorb the new reserve requirement

From 9 December, every bank must lock away an additional 1% of its rupee deposits at the Central Bank. Banks are profit driven hence will find the money, but the way they find it matters.

They will run down their buffers first. Banks still hold large liquid buffers, mostly in Government securities. Selling or not renewing Treasury bills will meet the requirement, but it will push up the Government’s borrowing costs.

Who will pay the price

Here lies the danger. The burden of this tightening will not fall evenly.

Most SME loans are linked to the lending rate and reprice immediately. Many consumer and vehicle loans carry fixed rates and do not. Gold-backed pawning loans are short-term, fully secured and remain highly profitable for banks. So the borrowers the Central Bank most wants to slow down, consumers buying cars and pawning gold, will feel the least. The borrowers it should most want to protect, the manufacturers, farmers and small traders who produce goods, will feel the most.

We already know how fragile this sector is. The Department of Census and Statistics found that 204,100 micro, small and medium enterprises had closed permanently by the end of 2022, with another 59,100 closed temporarily. The SME sector has never fully recovered from that blow, and it now faces higher rates again.

The vicious circle we must avoid

If the tightening falls hardest on producers, the consequences will follow one another:

This is the trap of fighting a supply shock with demand tools alone. Tighten too hard, and we reduce the supply of goods faster than we reduce the demand for them.

Meanwhile, the pressures from outside have not eased. The US Federal Reserve is raising rates, the rupee lost 6.8% against the dollar between January and October, and gross official reserves stood at about $ 7.1 billion at the end of October. The IMF program ends in March 2027. Every one of these makes the margin for error smaller.

What the Budget offers, and where it falls short

The 2027 Budget allocates about Rs. 68 billion for interest subsidies and refinancing to support    Rs. 174 billion of concessionary lending to micro, small and medium enterprises. That is welcome. But a subsidy designed at one level of interest rates loses value with every increase. The Government should review these schemes now, so that they still reach the businesses they were meant for.

What must be done instead

The Central Bank is right to act. But it should use sharper tools, and the Government must deal with the supply side, which monetary policy cannot reach.

Tier 1: Sharpen the monetary tools

Tier 2: Attack the supply shock

Three further measures should be prepared now, ready to be triggered without delay: restricting bank financing of vehicle imports, a phased withdrawal of the Rs. 5,000 note, and long-term certificates of deposit to draw idle money back into the banks. They matter even more now that deposits are scarce.

One foot on the accelerator, one on the brake

There is a further complication that has received little attention. While the Central Bank is trying to slow the flow of money, the Treasury is preparing to release a great deal of it.

The 2027 Budget allocates about Rs. 2 trillion to public investment, 5.1% of GDP. This year’s capital budget has gone largely unspent: by September, only about Rs. 385 billion of the Rs. 1,380 billion allocated had been used, roughly 28%. The Government says most of it will be spent in the final months of the year. Of the Rs. 1.75 trillion deficit planned for 2027, about Rs. 1.64 trillion is to be borrowed at home.

Whether this spending adds to inflation depends on three things.

The outcome could fall anywhere across four broad scenarios:

I have found no published assessment that brings the Treasury’s investment plans and the Central Bank’s tightening into a single picture. The Central Bank publishes its inflation projections. The Treasury publishes its fiscal position. But what happens to prices, interest rates and the rupee if both succeed at the same time?

The Treasury plans to spend Rs. 2 trillion. The Central Bank is trying to slow the flow of money. There is no visible joint plan for what happens when both succeed.

The Central Bank must see the whole picture

The Central Bank’s Economic Research Department should now model the supply side as closely as it models money and credit. What happens to output if SME borrowing costs rise by two percentage points? How many businesses close, and how many jobs are lost? How much does that reduce deposits? If a measure designed to cut inflation reduces production, it may end up raising the very prices it was meant to control.

These assessments must reach the Monetary Policy Board before decisions are made, not after. And the Central Bank and the Treasury must act together. Monetary policy can slow demand. Only fiscal and sectoral policy can restore supply.

A question of stewardship

Stewardship means taking over something that is not yours and leaving it in better shape than you found it. Our banking system is stronger today than it has been for years. The task now is to cool the credit boom without breaking the businesses that keep this economy producing, employing and exporting.

We cannot fight a fuel price shock by shutting down the businesses that make what we eat and sell.

Raising rates and reserves treats one half of the problem. If we ignore the other half, we may find ourselves with less money, fewer goods, and prices that are still rising.

(The author is a former senior banker, Regional Director of CIMA for the Middle East, South Asia and North Africa, Head of PPP (2017), and has served on two national Education Reform Commissions)

title: From policy to protection: Why justice must be a right, not a privilege | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 03:47
-     - 19

Sri Lanka has made commendable progress. We must recognise these achievements, build upon them and find the collective courage to address what remains unfinished. Success will be defined when fewer women experience violence, when survivors seek help without fear, and when every woman and girl lives with uncompromised dignity and freedom

As we mark the beginning of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence on 25 November, I find myself reflecting on a simple yet heartbreaking question: What does a woman or girl truly endure when she takes the courageous step to seek justice after facing gender-based violence (GBV)? What do safety and freedom really feel like when the very spaces meant to protect her fail to do so?

For far too many women, the ordeal begins right in their own home: the very place where they ought to feel safest becomes a place of fear and violence. Meanwhile, the family and community they call their own and rely on for protection prevent them from seeking justice and sanction them for doing so. When violence strikes at home, they confront overwhelming familial and social pressures and coercion from family and community members to stay silent and settle matters privately, and they are overwhelmed with anxiety about the wellbeing of their children, their careers and their family’s reputation.

Yet when they find the courage to step out of their homes and report the violence, a new wave of challenges awaits. From their homes to the police station, hospital and courtroom, they encounter systemic barriers: dismissive attitudes, pressure to reconcile, language barriers, a lack of privacy and of female officials, invasive and insensitive examinations, and limited awareness of laws and rights amongst survivors. This is compounded by the severe financial and mental strain resulting from prolonged and endless legal procedures and the repeated recounting and reliving of trauma. The overwhelming burden of seeking justice falls almost entirely on the survivor herself.

Silence behind the numbers

Sri Lanka’s 2019 National Women’s Wellbeing Survey reveals the true gravity of these challenges. One in five ever-partnered women (20.4%) has experienced physical and/or sexual violence by an intimate partner in her lifetime, while two in five (39.8%) have endured physical, sexual, emotional or economic violence, or controlling behaviours. Most heartbreaking of all, nearly half (49.3%) of women who survived sexual violence by a partner never sought formal help.

Behind these numbers is a mother, daughter or sister who feared being blamed, judged or disbelieved. They are women who worry about their children’s future, financial survival and community backlash, and women who endured the abuse because it had been normalised for generations.

What must we do to dismantle these barriers and make seeking justice a seamless, empowering path for every survivor?

From law to practice

Despite persistent challenges, Sri Lanka has made important strides towards advancing the rights and empowerment of women. The National Policy on Gender Equality and Women’s Empowerment (2023-2033) and the Women Empowerment Act, No. 37 of 2024, mark significant milestones in this journey. They demonstrate the Government’s resolve to move beyond declarations towards robust institutional protections and gender equality. The enactment of the Women Empowerment Act provides a vital foundation for accountability, notably through the establishment of the National Commission on Women.

However, legislation and policy only result in meaningful progress and benefit society if they are effectively enforced or implemented. Sri Lanka already possesses a critical legal framework, including the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act, the Victims and Witnesses Protection Act, police support units and specialised survivor services. Our immediate task is ensuring these mechanisms operate seamlessly together, receive adequate resources and remain accessible to every woman, creating safer spaces everywhere.

We must also identify and acknowledge remaining legal and practical gaps, ensuring robust protection extends to all forms of abuse, especially technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV), which increasingly targets women and girls online. Equally vital is prevention. Violence begins long before a physical act: entrenched harmful social norms perpetuate and normalise abuse, taking root in everyday attitudes that excuse digital harassment, coercion and unequal power dynamics.

Ending violence requires connecting Government commitments to a powerful public narrative. Sri Lanka possesses deeply ingrained cultural values of respect, protection, care and dignity for women. We must draw on these values to nurture children who understand consent, build communities that firmly reject violence, and engage men and boys as active partners in positive change. No woman should ever have to alter how she dresses, travels, works or lives simply to stay safe and free from violence.

Justice every day

This year’s national theme, #JusticeIsMyRight: UNiTE Towards Ending GBV, is both a solemn promise and an urgent call to action. Government institutions, civil society and local communities must immediately channel Sri Lanka’s capacity for progress into decisive, tangible action. Our solidarity cannot expire on December 10; it must be actively proven every day in every police station, hospital, courtroom, digital platform and neighbourhood.

UNFPA has supported the Government of Sri Lanka in these efforts, providing technical and financial assistance for the National Gender Equality and Women’s Empowerment Policy and technical support towards the Women Empowerment Act and its strategic action plan. We remain dedicated to accompanying national partners in translating these legislative milestones into lasting, progressive change.

Sri Lanka has made commendable progress. We must recognise these achievements, build upon them and find the collective courage to address what remains unfinished. Success will be defined when fewer women experience violence, when survivors seek help without fear, and when every woman and girl lives with uncompromised dignity and freedom.

Justice must never be something a woman has to fight endlessly to achieve; it must be a right she can confidently expect. That is the promise of #JusticeIsMyRight, and together, we must fulfil it.

(The author is UNFPA Representative a.i. in Sri Lanka)

title: Dengue: A persistent national  threat demanding year-round action | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 03:42
-     - 26

Dengue has become an all-too-familiar part of life in Sri Lanka. Each year, particularly with the arrival of the monsoon rains, rising case numbers prompt renewed public concern, mosquito-control campaigns and calls for greater vigilance. Yet, as the immediate threat subsides, public attention often diminishes, only to return with the next outbreak.

This recurring pattern raises an important question: Have we begun to accept dengue as an inevitable part of life, rather than a preventable public health threat that demands sustained national action?

For decades, dengue has remained one of Sri Lanka’s most persistent public health challenges. Despite considerable progress in disease surveillance, clinical management and vector control, it continues to impose a substantial burden on individuals, families, healthcare institutions and the national economy.

The magnitude of this challenge is evident in our epidemiological experience. In 2017, Sri Lanka experienced its largest recorded dengue epidemic, with 186,101 suspected cases and 440 reported deaths. Nearly a decade later, the country continues to face significant outbreaks, demonstrating that dengue remains far from being brought under sustainable control.

The situation in 2026 is particularly concerning. According to surveillance figures reported in November, Sri Lanka had recorded 110,431 dengue cases and 82 deaths by November 2026. The Western Province continued to bear a disproportionate burden, while transmission remained a concern across the country.

These figures represent much more than epidemiological statistics. Behind every reported case is an individual whose health, education or livelihood may be disrupted, a family experiencing anxiety and, in severe cases, a patient requiring intensive medical care. Every preventable death is a reminder that dengue remains a potentially fatal disease, even in a country with extensive experience in its clinical management.

Early recognition

Early recognition and timely medical intervention are therefore critical. Dengue commonly presents with fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea and sometimes a rash. However, the most dangerous period may begin as the fever subsides, when some patients enter the critical phase of illness.

Warning signs such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, marked lethargy, restlessness or signs of circulatory compromise require urgent medical assessment. Patients with suspected dengue should seek timely medical advice, maintain appropriate hydration and avoid medications such as aspirin and ibuprofen because of the risk of bleeding. Early identification, careful monitoring and appropriate fluid management can substantially reduce the risk of death.

Importantly, dengue is no longer a concern confined to Colombo or other densely populated urban centres. Although the Western Province accounts for a substantial proportion of cases, the disease affects communities across Sri Lanka. Rapid urbanisation, inadequate waste management, construction activities, population movement, rainfall patterns and environmental conditions all contribute to the persistence and spread of mosquito breeding sites.

Changing weather patterns and increasing climatic variability further complicate dengue prevention. However, rainfall alone does not explain the problem. Poor environmental management, neglected premises, improperly stored water and inadequate community participation create conditions that allow mosquito populations to thrive.

Fundamental challenge

The fundamental challenge is therefore not simply controlling dengue during an outbreak but preventing the conditions that allow repeated outbreaks to occur.

Sri Lanka has developed considerable expertise in dengue management, supported by dedicated healthcare professionals, public health teams and national surveillance systems. The National Dengue Control Unit and other health authorities have played an important role in coordinating prevention and response activities. Nevertheless, the continuing burden of disease demonstrates that healthcare-sector interventions alone cannot provide a lasting solution.

Dengue prevention must become a shared national responsibility.

Every household should routinely inspect its surroundings and eliminate potential mosquito breeding sites. Water-collecting containers, discarded tyres, blocked gutters, flowerpots, construction materials and improperly managed waste require particular attention. Water-storage containers must be securely covered and regularly cleaned. Personal protection through appropriate clothing, mosquito repellents and measures to prevent mosquito bites during the day should also be encouraged.

However, individual responsibility, while essential, is insufficient without supportive public systems.

Local authorities must ensure effective solid-waste management, drainage maintenance and environmental sanitation. Schools and workplaces should adopt regular, structured dengue-prevention programmes rather than limiting activities to periods of heightened transmission. Construction sites abandoned buildings and public spaces require systematic monitoring and accountability.

Equally important is strengthening coordination between the health sector, local government, education authorities, environmental agencies, community organisations and the private sector. Dengue control should be embedded within routine institutional responsibilities, supported by clear accountability, reliable surveillance and timely action.

Sri Lanka’s National Dengue Review in August 2026 reinforced the importance of evidence-based interventions, stronger operational coordination, sustained preparedness and active community participation. These priorities should now translate into measurable action at national, provincial, district and community levels.

Proactive approach 

A more proactive approach is essential. Surveillance data, mosquito breeding indices, weather information and local epidemiological trends should be used to identify high-risk areas and guide targeted interventions before outbreaks escalate. Public communication must also move beyond occasional warnings towards sustained education that encourages practical behavioural change.

Ultimately, successful dengue control should not be measured solely by the number of emergency campaigns conducted or premises inspected during an outbreak. It should be judged by sustained reductions in transmission, preventable hospitalisations and deaths, supported by healthier and safer environments.

Sri Lanka has demonstrated its capacity to achieve remarkable public health outcomes through strong preventive services, community engagement and coordinated national programmes. The same commitment must now be directed towards dengue.

The goal should not merely be to respond effectively to the next dengue outbreak, but to prevent that outbreak from occurring wherever possible.

Dengue does not respect administrative boundaries, socioeconomic divisions or seasonal public health priorities. Our response must therefore be continuous, coordinated and inclusive.

The responsibility extends beyond the Ministry of Health. It belongs to every institution, every community and every citizen.

Dengue may be a year-round threat but preventing it must become a year-round national commitment.
