title: Men’s mental health: Battles we never see | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 03:39
-     - 19

“Who supports the man who is expected to support everyone else?”

Men are often expected to be strong, dependable and emotionally resilient. From a young age, many boys grow up hearing phrases such as “boys don’t cry” or “be strong”. While these words may be intended to encourage resilience, they can unintentionally teach men that expressing emotions is a sign of weakness.

As we observe Men’s Mental Health Awareness Month this November, it is important to recognise that behind a confident smile, a successful career or a seemingly happy family, a man may be silently struggling. In my field of work as a psychologist, I have observed that men often find it difficult to express emotional distress. 

Instead of saying, “I am overwhelmed,” they may become irritable, withdrawn, unusually quiet or emotionally distant. Some immerse themselves in work, while others turn to alcohol, excessive screen time or other unhealthy coping mechanisms to escape what they are feeling.

Depression in men does not always look like sadness. Sometimes it appears as anger, frustration, exhaustion or a sudden lack of interest in relationships and activities they once enjoyed. 

Society often measures a man’s worth by his ability to provide, protect and succeed. Financial pressures, relationship difficulties, career expectations and family responsibilities can leave men feeling that failure is simply not an option. Unfortunately, many suffer in silence because they fear being judged or perceived as weak. 

True courage does not lie in denying these emotions, but in recognising them, understanding the mind and finding the strength to move forward. We must also recognise that men need emotional support just as much as women do. A husband needs to feel heard, a father needs reassurance, a son needs encouragement and a friend may simply need someone who listens without judgement.

Seeking psychological support is not a sign of weakness. It is an act of courage and responsibility towards oneself and one’s loved ones. This Men’s Mental Health Awareness Month, perhaps we should change the conversation. Instead of constantly reminding men to be strong, let us remind them that they are allowed to be human. After all, a man’s greatest strength lies not in how much pain he can carry in silence, but in knowing when he no longer has to carry it alone.

title: What’s in a name? Why NMRA must hold the line on unlabelled filgrastim | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 26 November 2026 00:21
-     - 20

The NMRA’s decision will reach far beyond one consignment. If a missing product name can be patched with stickers in a warehouse, every supplier learns that labelling is negotiable once the stock has landed. If the regulator holds the line, suppliers learn to get it right before they ship. Sri Lanka is also building a local pharmaceutical industry that aims to export, and that ambition rests on the credibility of its regulator. Overseas buyers and inspectors judge a country’s medicines by how its regulator behaves under pressure

Umpire Ross Emerson tested the character of Arjuna Ranatunga’s captaincy in 1999. In 2026, quarantined consignment of temperature-sensitive (2–8 °C) injectable biological medicine is testing the character of Sri Lanka’s regulatory authority.

A missing name

In a cold store in Sri Lanka, a large Government-tender consignment of filgrastim pre-filled syringes sits in quarantine. Filgrastim helps protect patients on chemotherapy from dangerous, sometimes fatal, infections by shortening severe neutropenia (a dangerously low white blood cell count).

The outer cartons of this consignment are fully labelled but the syringes inside are not. Each syringe carries its strength, batch number, manufacturing date and expiry date, but not the name of the medicine or the name of its maker. Now this might not seem worth all the fuss to the average consumer. I know I’ve bought groceries plenty of times not knowing the brand or maker as long as I knew the expiry date and ingredients. But this is not a supermarket; these aren’t groceries; and the accountability of manufacturers when it comes to biological medicines is little more essential than when it comes to your jam and butter.

The supplier has asked to fix this by labelling the syringes here, in Sri Lanka, under the eye of regulatory officers. The National Medicines Regulatory Authority (‘NMRA’) has rightly refused to decide in haste. It is understood that NMRA’s Medicines Evaluation Committee has asked for the views of the Attorney General’s Department and the World Health Organisation on the request.

Historically I have been very candid and very critical of the NMRA, its actions and its rationale for those actions. But this time, its caution and adherence to protocol deserves support and appreciation.

Why does the name belong on the syringe?

Both global and domestic standards require these to be labelled on both the outer box and the inner container. Clear identification on every syringe is also basic to pharmacovigilance; it lets adverse reactions be reported and traced quickly, and lets the medicine’s use and quality be monitored: the WHO’s good manufacturing practice (‘GMP’) principles require every finished medicine to be labelled with its name; Article 55 of the European Union’s Directive 2001/83/EC requires the name even on the smallest immediate container, where nothing else will fit; and the NMRA’s own registration of this product makes it mandatory on the primary pack.

The reason is practical, not bureaucratic. A carton protects the syringes in a warehouse. In a ward, it is opened, and the syringes go into trays, fridges and nurses’ hands. From that moment, the syringe must speak for itself. A nurse preparing an injection at 2 AM reads the syringe, not the box it came in. A syringe that says only ‘300 mcg’ and a batch code could be mistaken for any injection of a similar strength. Medication mix-ups like this are exactly what labelling rules exist to prevent.

The supplier says the batch number and expiry date keep the product traceable. True, but traceability is not identification. A batch code tells you, after the fact, what went wrong. A name stops it going wrong in the first place.

Why is labelling here not advisable?

The proposed fix carries more risk than the fault it is meant to cure. Labelling a sterile biological medicine is not clerical work. It is a manufacturing step. The WHO’s GMP principles treat labelling as part of production, and anyone who does it as a manufacturer. That work belongs in a licensed site, with validated procedures, trained staff, full batch records and temperature control. An importer’s warehouse is none of these.

The practical risks are serious. The first is the cold chain. Filgrastim is a protein that must stay between 2°C and 8°C, and handling tens of thousands of syringes outside a controlled packaging line invites temperature excursions that may leave no visible trace. Every syringe taken out and put back also risks a cracked barrel, a loosened cap, or a compromised seal.

Then there are the labels themselves. The consignment spans five batches. Hand-applying loose labels across five batches is a classic recipe for the wrong batch number on the wrong syringe, which is why GMP prefers roll-fed labels to loose cut ones. A licensed site would also reconcile every label issued, used and destroyed. Recreating that discipline in a temporary set-up is hard, and any gap undermines confidence in every syringe. Supervision cannot substitute for a qualified facility. An inspector can watch a process. An inspector cannot validate it.

The shortage is real, but so are the safer options

Although interim precautions have been put in place, while the NMRA deliberates the way forward, no one should dismiss the possibility of a shortage. Patients on chemotherapy need filgrastim, and every week of delay matters. The Medical Supplies Division (‘MSD’) has arranged an urgent air-freighted quantity, and hospitals have been authorised to buy locally. But a shortage is an argument for speed, not for lower standards. There are faster, safer routes than a DIY warehouse labelling line.

First, test independently. Samples from every batch should be tested by a qualified laboratory before a single syringe reaches a patient. Second, labelling should be done at a licensed site, or replace the stock. If the syringes are sound, the manufacturer should relabel them at its own licensed facility; if not, they should be exported back and replaced. Third, bridge the gap in the meantime with emergency procurement of correctly labelled, registered stock (now, here is the right occasion to bring medicine down using emergency regulations).

Finally, close the procurement gap. The manufacturer says the Government-specific artwork was approved by the procurement side before production. If so, tender artwork must in future be checked against the NMRA-registered labelling before anything is made. The NMRA has already told the State Pharmaceuticals Corporation (‘SPC’) that sticker labels are not acceptable in line with its own labelling guideline, GL-006, which allows over-stickers only for the name in national languages and the price, subject to NMRA pre-approval. That rule should be in every tender.

What will the decision signal?

The NMRA’s decision will reach far beyond one consignment. If a missing product name can be patched with stickers in a warehouse, every supplier learns that labelling is negotiable once the stock has landed. If the regulator holds the line, suppliers learn to get it right before they ship.

Sri Lanka is also building a local pharmaceutical industry that aims to export, and that ambition rests on the credibility of its regulator. Overseas buyers and inspectors judge a country’s medicines by how its regulator behaves under

pressure.

The Medicines Evaluation Committee has taken the right first step by seeking legal and WHO advice before acting. It should now insist on independent testing, labelling or re-labelling only at a licensed facility, and approved labels in every future tender.

The same way Ranatunga stood up for Muralitharan in Adelaide all those years ago, patients will laude a regulator that stands up for them, and doesn’t expect them to trust a syringe that cannot say what it is.

(The author is an attorney-at-law)

Sri Lanka emerged champions of the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy 2026 when they beat Ireland by six wickets in the final played at Karwan Sports Club Ground, Ajman yesterday.

Ireland, who won all three of their Super Six matches to reach the final, were bowled out for 96 after being put into bat, and Sri Lanka reached their target with 44 balls to spare.

Hunter was then dismissed lbw to Sugandika Kumari, Laura Delany (7) was run out and Abbi Harrison (5) was stumped off Nimasha Meepage as Ireland slipped to 54-6 in the 12th over. 

Alana Dalzell (24) and Georgina Dempsey (13) added 28 for the seventh wicket before Dempsey was run out in the 16th over. Sandeepani then removed Cara Murray (3) and Dalzell in the 18th over, and Chethana Vimukthi bowled Kia McCartney (1) as Ireland were bowled out for 96 in 19.3 overs. 

In reply, Sanjana Kavindi (25) and Vishmi Gunaratne (10) added 35 for the first wicket, but McCartney (2/16) removed Kavindi and captain Harshitha Samarawickrama (0) off successive balls in the sixth over. title: Sri Lanka ‘A’ come up against destructive Sooryavanshi | Daily FT
summary:

Unbeaten Sri Lanka ‘A’, led by Pavan Rathnayake, will face their first real test when they front up against India ‘A’ in the first semi-final of the Asia Cup Rising Stars 50-over tournament in Doha today.

The challenge for the Sri Lanka ‘A’ bowlers is to get the wicket of destructive opener Vaibhav Sooryavanshi early, because he can take the game away from the opposition on his own, as he showed two days ago by smashing the fastest double century in List A cricket, off 53 balls, against UAE.

India ‘A’s batting is not all about Sooryavanshi, although he has grabbed the headlines with his extraordinary batting. They have a strong line-up that will test the Lankan ‘A’ bowlers, who have been pretty good so far, dismissing Afghanistan ‘A’ for 139 and Bangladesh ‘A’ for 145. Only against Hong Kong did they come up against strong opposition, conceding 260, but Sri Lanka ‘A’ still managed to win that game by 24 runs.

In Captain Tilak Varma and Kumar Kushagra, India ‘A’ have two batters who have scored centuries in the tournament. Abhishek Sharma and Shahbaz Ahmed have also each crossed the fifty-run mark once.

Sri Lanka ‘A’s bowling has relied mostly on spin, with Wanuja Sahan, Ravindra Fernando, Vijayakanth Viyaskanth, Chamika Heenatigala and Nipun Dananjaya playing a big role in their victories, supported by the left-arm seam of Dulaj Samuditha. India ‘A’s attack is based mainly on seam, with Prince Yadav, Harshit Rana and Arshad Khan their key wicket-takers.

Sri Lanka ‘A’s batting has been tested only once. Against Afghanistan ‘A’ they batted first and ran up 284-9, but in their other two group games they were chasing small totals and were never properly stretched.

Opener Lasith Croospulle, one-drop batter Nishan Madushka, skipper Pavan Rathnayake and Janith Liyanage have been the main contributors to the Lankan ‘A’ totals, with Croospulle’s 75 against Hong Kong the highest score.

Opener Sineth Jayawardena needs to curb his early aggression and not try to hit every ball he receives out of the park. Once set, he can go after the bowling. This is not a 20-over game but a 50-over one, and there is plenty of time to play yourself in before unleashing your full repertoire of strokes.

India ‘A’ suffered one loss on their way to the semi-finals, against arch rivals Pakistan ‘A’, but wins over Nepal and UAE secured them a place in the last four. Pakistan ‘A’ are the only other team to remain unbeaten in the tournament, finishing top of Group B with three wins. They play Bangladesh ‘A’ in the second semi-final on Friday. The final is scheduled for Sunday. (ST)

Prima Group Sri Lanka Under-15 Sri Lanka Youth League 2026 will be played from today (26) till 5 December, with the final at the MCA Ground on 5 December.

Organised by Prima Group Sri Lanka in partnership with Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) under the National Pathway Program, the 50-over tournament will feature five Super Provincial teams representing Colombo North, Colombo South, Dambulla, Galle, and Kandy in the Under-15 segment. Matches will be played across four grounds in Colombo, with the semi-finals on 3 December before the final on 5 December.

Prima Group Sri Lanka continues its commitment to youth cricket as Title Sponsor for the 19th year, having supported the tournament since 2007. Formerly known as the Prima Champions Cup, the competition has provided a platform for thousands of young cricketers to represent their provinces and progress towards national honours. Several participants have gone on to represent Sri Lanka. Prima provides nutrients, materials, and cricket attire for players. After the completion of the tournament, 26 young cricketers will be selected for the national Under-15 squad.

SLC Head of Marketing Upul Nawarathna Bandara said the tournament helps identify promising talent and develop future national cricketers. Prima Group Ceylon Agro Industries General Manager Sajith Gunaratne said the league is a significant platform for discovering emerging talent, adding that Prima is proud to support grassroots cricket through its longstanding partnership with SLC for 19 long years.

Teams: Kandy, Galle, Dambulla, Colombo North, Colombo South

Date: 26 November - 5 December

Venues: MCA, Colombo University Ground, Ananda Ground, Royal Ground
